events.note: this plan assumed `Account` already had a movement collection to extend ("balance stays derived as the sum of movements ... never assigned directly") — actually `Account` is `class Account(val number: AccountNumber)` with `balance()` returning the constant `BigDecimal.ZERO` and no movement collection at all — SCENARIO-01's *code* was the source: its own plan said "keep the aggregate's movement-derivation shape ready to extend", and the implementation instead hardcoded the constant. The collection is introduced here.

row 5 assumed SCENARIO-01 "pinned the projection with an empty movement list" — actually SCENARIO-01's row 7 asserts `number` and `balance` as two separate field assertions and never mentions movements — SCENARIO-01's *code* was the source (its plan did call row 7 a full-projection row). Row 5 is therefore written as a new contract test rather than an edit of row 7's test, so the two rows stay 1:1 with two test methods.

this plan assumed `Movement` needed no structural change because it "already models a typed movement" — actually `MovementType` is an enum with a single `DEPOSIT` constant, so a `WITHDRAWAL` constant had to be added along with a `Movement.withdrawal(...)` factory — SCENARIO-02's *code* was the source: its plan only promised a `Movement` that "records a `DEPOSIT` with its amount", and the implementation chose to express the kind as a one-constant enum.

this plan assumed "balance stays derived as the sum of movements" carried over unchanged — actually `Account.balance()` folds each movement's raw `amount`, so summing an unsigned withdrawal *raises* the balance; a `Movement.signedAmount()` was introduced and `balance()` now folds that — SCENARIO-02's *code* was the source, which had no reason to distinguish sign with only deposits in existence.

the plan assumed `withdraw` held the positivity guard inline, so the balance guard would be "evaluated after" it — actually SCENARIO-04 extracted the positivity guard into a shared private `record(amount, movement)` used by both `deposit` and `withdraw`, so `exceedsBalance` is evaluated *before* it (equivalent: a non-positive amount never exceeds a non-negative balance, and `fails_when_the_withdrawn_amount_is_negative` still passes) — predecessor's code was the source.

the plan placed `InsufficientBalanceException` in the same *file* as `Account` — actually every exception in this package has its own file (`NonPositiveAmountException.kt`, `AccountAlreadyExistsException.kt`), so it got `InsufficientBalanceException.kt` — predecessor's code was the source.

the plan assumed the adapter spec could take the contract's new `breakSavingOf` hook as a plain public test class — actually SCENARIO-01 declared `AccountJpaRepository` `internal`, so the hook's delegating JPA repository and the adapter spec itself both had to become `internal` — code was the source (a predecessor's implementation choice the plan did not carry).

the plan assumed the adapter's decode of a legacy row *fails* (catch/skip a throwing row) — actually the current schema has no way to express a pre-movements record at all, so one had to be added (`AccountEntity.stored_balance`, nullable, never written) and decoding it never throws; the skip is a recognised-and-returned-null, not a caught exception — the plan was the source (it predicted a mechanism the schema does not have).

the plan assumed the contract could freely `save` ACC-002 — actually SCENARIO-06's `BreakableAccountJpaRepository` keeps refusing a number for the rest of the class once `breakSavingOf` is called, so row 1 reddened on a leaked refusal; the adapter suite's before-each now resets it — a predecessor's code was the source.

the Structure section says "SCENARIO-07's statement read is explicitly out of scope for this scenario per its own plan; leave it unguarded" — actually SCENARIO-07's plan says the opposite ("Account-not-found handling … deferred to SCENARIO-09", and it lists `returns_404_when_the_account_does_not_exist` as "SCENARIO-09's red arrival") — the *plan* was the source: this scenario's architect mis-read a predecessor's plan, not its code. Row 6's note-to-architect is authoritative and was followed; the controller is guarded here.
